input_text: This film asks three questions. What does the text actually say? What did the earliest scholars understand by it? And what, if anything, has archaeology really found?

input_text: To answer them, we must keep different kinds of evidence apart: scripture, scholarship, legend, excavation and hypothesis. Throughout this film, each will be marked as it appears.

input_text: The Quran names عَاد twenty-four times. إِرَم, it names only once.

input_text: In the Quranic account, عَاد were a people who came after the people of Noah. To them was sent a prophet from among themselves. The Quran calls him their brother: Hood.

input_text: It describes a people blessed with plenty. Hood reminds them that God has aided them with cattle and sons, and gardens and watersprings.

display_text: He reminds them that they were given "growth of stature": in Arabic, basṭa, a word the commentators read as size, or strength, or reach.

input_text: They were builders. Build ye on every high place a monument for vain delight? Hood asks them. And seek ye out strongholds, that haply ye may last for ever?

input_text: What the Quran does not give us is a date, a map, or a description of a city. It gives a moral history: a people given strength and plenty; a warning; a refusal.

input_text: Arabia, in other words, was not always this dry. Over many thousands of years, its landscapes have shifted between green and gold.

input_text: But we should be clear. These changes unfolded over centuries and millennia. No study has dated the people of عَاد, and no geological event has been shown to match the Quranic account.

input_text: At Shisr, the excavators found no evidence that a sandstorm destroyed the site. The collapse of its fortress into a sinkhole has a geological explanation, and no known connection to عَاد.

input_text: Religious memory and physical evidence are answering different questions. Merging them would do justice to neither.

input_text: In recent years, the search for إِرَم has taken an unexpected turn, away from the southern sands altogether.

input_text: In the deserts of southern Jordan lies Wadi Ramm, the valley known today as Wadi Rum: red cliffs, and some twenty thousand recorded inscriptions.
display_text: In the deserts of southern Jordan lies Wadi Ramm, the valley known today as Wadi Rum: red cliffs, and some twenty thousand recorded inscriptions.

input_text: A Nabataean temple to the goddess Allat stands at the foot of Jabal Ramm, and inscriptions from the site give the ancient name of the place as إِرَم.
display_text: A Nabataean temple to the goddess Allat stands at the foot of Jabal Ramm, and inscriptions from the site give the ancient name of the place as Iram.

input_text: In two thousand and twenty-five, the epigrapher Ahmad Al-Jallad published a study of pre-Islamic inscriptions written by members of a tribe called عَاد, in the deserts of the north, and argued that the Quranic names may belong to this region.
display_text: In two thousand and twenty-five, the epigrapher Ahmad Al-Jallad published a study of pre-Islamic inscriptions written by members of a tribe called ʿĀd, in the deserts of the north, and argued that the Quranic names may belong to this region.

input_text: It is a serious proposal, built on careful readings of ancient texts. It is also new, and scholars are still weighing it. Like Shisr before it, it shows how much depends on the evidence we choose to follow.
display_text: It is a serious proposal, built on careful readings of ancient texts. It is also new, and scholars are still weighing it. Like Shisr before it, it shows how much depends on the evidence we choose to follow.

input_text: So, what can we actually say?
display_text: So, what can we actually say?

input_text: The Quran tells of a people named عَاد; of their prophet, Hood; of their strength and their building; and of a wind that left only their dwellings. It names إِرَم once, and calls it dhaat al-ee-maad.
display_text: The Quran tells of a people named ʿĀd; of their prophet, Hūd; of their strength and their building; and of a wind that left only their dwellings. It names Iram once, and calls it dhāt al-ʿimād.

input_text: The classical scholars recorded a debate. Two of the most influential, al-Tabari and Ibn Katheer, understood إِرَم as a tribe, and its ee-maad as the poles of tents. And they rejected the legend of a golden city.
display_text: The classical scholars recorded a debate. Two of the most influential, al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr, understood Iram as a tribe, and its ʿimād as the poles of tents. And they rejected the legend of a golden city.

input_text: Archaeology has found real places: a caravan fortress at Shisr, frankincense ports on the coast, and, in the north, inscriptions that name both إِرَم and a tribe called عَاد. It has not found a city of a thousand pillars.
display_text: Archaeology has found real places: a caravan fortress at Shisr, frankincense ports on the coast, and, in the north, inscriptions that name both Iram and a tribe called ʿĀd. It has not found a city of a thousand pillars.

input_text: And some things remain unknown: when عَاد lived; exactly where; and what their pillars really were.
display_text: And some things remain unknown: when ʿĀd lived; exactly where; and what their pillars really were.

input_text: Perhaps that is the real lesson of إِرَم. A people can survive in memory long after their stones are gone, or even if they never built in stone at all. A few words in a sacred text have outlived empires, maps and explorers.
display_text: Perhaps that is the real lesson of Iram. A people can survive in memory long after their stones are gone, or even if they never built in stone at all. A few words in a sacred text have outlived empires, maps and explorers.

input_text: The wind still moves across the sand, as it always has, erasing footprints by evening. What remains is the question. And the discipline to tell the difference between what we know, what we believe, and what we only imagine.
